stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy uses one ADD only as an approved emergency medication kit and a second ADD for routine medication dispensing. A licensed nurse asks to load both machines. Which answer best applies under the current ADD policy?
choices: The nurse is an authorized loader for the emergency-kit ADD, but the routine-dispensing ADD uses the policy's certified-pharmacy-technician or pharmacy-intern loading pathway under pharmacist supervision.
The policy gives different loader lists for emergency-kit and routine retail ADD use.
The nurse may load both machines because licensure as a nurse overrides the purpose of the ADD.
Routine retail dispensing has a narrower stated loader pathway.
The nurse may load neither machine because only pharmacists may load any ADD.
A licensed nurse is listed for emergency-kit or similar approved use.
The nurse may load the routine machine only when it contains Schedule VI drugs.
Routine loader eligibility is not converted by limiting inventory to Schedule VI.
The two machines follow identical loading rules because both are owned by the same pharmacy.
Device purpose changes the applicable loading rule.
steps: Classify each ADD by emergency-kit versus routine-dispensing use
Apply the distinct loader rule for each mode
core: Massachusetts distinguishes emergency-kit ADD loading from routine retail ADD loading; licensed nurses are listed for the former, while the latter uses supervised certified-technician or intern loading.
facts: Routine retail ADDs also carry machine-specific registration and continuous-video requirements.
trap: Assuming one authorized emergency-kit loader automatically has the same authority for routine dispensing.
distinct: Tests device-purpose classification rather than the drug/schedule loader matrix in Q0183.
anti_guess: All options keep the same nurse and machines; the candidate must distinguish ADD mode rather than recognize a drug schedule.

stem: Every option below involves gabapentin stock at an otherwise eligible Massachusetts hospital ADD. Which stocking actions are permitted under the current technician-stocking policy? Select all that apply.
choices: A pharmacy technician trainee loads pharmacist-verified gabapentin using required electronic validation under pharmacist direction and supervision.
A PTT may load pharmacist-verified Schedule III-VI stock; gabapentin is Massachusetts Schedule VI.
A licensed non-trainee pharmacy technician loads pharmacist-verified gabapentin using electronic validation under pharmacist supervision.
The licensed-technician pathway permits verified Schedule II-VI stock.
A nationally certified licensed technician uses the no-prior-pharmacist-verification Schedule VI shortcut for gabapentin.
That narrow shortcut excludes PMP drugs such as gabapentin.
A nationally certified licensed technician loads pharmacist-verified gabapentin under the ordinary supervised licensed-technician pathway.
National certification does not prevent use of the ordinary verified-stock pathway.
A pharmacy technician trainee loads unverified gabapentin based only on a visual bottle check.
The PTT pathway requires pharmacist-verified stock plus electronic validation.
steps: Classify the technician credential and verification pathway
Apply the PMP exclusion only to the no-prior-verification shortcut
core: Gabapentin can be handled through the ordinary verified-stock technician pathways, but its PMP status excludes it from the nationally certified technician's narrow no-prior-verification Schedule VI shortcut.
facts: Gabapentin remains Massachusetts Schedule VI while being PMP-reportable.
trap: Turning the gabapentin PMP exclusion into a blanket ban on all technician stocking.
distinct: Replaces the earlier near-duplicate multi-drug eligibility matrix with a same-drug actor/pathway matrix.
anti_guess: The drug never changes; each option requires independent actor, verification, and PMP-pathway classification.
